Question: Walk through how the hail loss reaches Westmere Networks Group's balance sheet and covenants. Show your steps and give a verdict.

Sources:
[1] Scenario: Westmere Networks Group owns a chain of retail warehouses. Hazard: hail. All money is in millions of one currency.

[2] Financials before the event: revenue 1,441.6; EBITDA 506.3; net debt 276.8; interest expense 12.7; equity 225.2; total assets 1,439.8.

[3] Loss inputs: asset damage 70.2; insured recovery 63.2; extra costs 23.8.

[4] Covenants: EBITDA/interest at least 36.10x.

[5] Engine result, loss: uninsured asset loss 7.0; EBITDA hit 23.8; pre-tax loss 30.8, which is 6.1% of EBITDA; share of the loss that is uninsured 0.0%.

[6] Engine result, after the loss: EBITDA 482.5; net debt 307.6; net debt/EBITDA 0.64x (was 0.55x); EBITDA/interest 37.99x (was 39.87x); equity/total assets 14.2% (was 15.6%).

[7] Engine result, covenant tests: EBITDA/interest 37.99x against a limit of at least 36.10x: pass, under 15% headroom, headroom 5.2%; before the loss it was a pass.

[8] Engine assumptions: the uninsured cash cost is funded by new debt; interest expense is unchanged; no covenant waiver, cure right, equity injection or insurer prepayment is assumed.

[9] Winter Storm Uri and the Texas power market (case summary): the driver was extreme cold causing generator and gas-supply outages; the exposed assets were power generators, retail electricity providers and cooperatives in the ERCOT market; the event took place in North America in 2021.

[10] Winter Storm Uri and the Texas power market (Vistra Form 10-Q, June 2023): ERCOT was left roughly $2.9 billion short after the storm, mostly because of Brazos, and filed a claim of about $1.9 billion against Brazos.

STEP 1 [FACT] Westmere Networks Group faces a hail loss with asset damage of 70.2, insured recovery of 63.2 and extra costs of 23.8 [3].
STEP 2 [FACT] The engine puts the uninsured asset loss at 7.0 and the EBITDA hit at 23.8, so the pre-tax loss is 30.8, which is 6.1% of EBITDA [5].
STEP 3 [INFERENCE from 2] The loss is meaningful but within what a year of earnings can absorb; it is driven by business interruption and extra cost, and insurance covers only part of the damage.
STEP 4 [FACT] After the loss EBITDA is 482.5 and net debt is 307.6; net debt/EBITDA moves from 0.55x to 0.64x [6].
STEP 5 [FACT] The EBITDA/interest test is 37.99x against a limit of at least 36.10x: pass, under 15% headroom with headroom of 5.2%; before the loss it was a pass [7].
STEP 6 [INFERENCE from 5] No covenant is breached, but EBITDA/interest is within 15% of its limit, so a slightly larger loss or a slower insurance payment could tip it.
STEP 7 [PRECEDENT] In Winter Storm Uri and the Texas power market: the driver was extreme cold causing generator and gas-supply outages [9].
STEP 8 [INFERENCE from 7, 3] Analysis (not stated in the sources): past cases suggest checking a shortage of an input such as power, water, transport or feedstock, price moves in the markets the firm sells into or buys from and pressure on credit ratings, liquidity and capital raising as well as direct damage.
STEP 9 [CAVEAT] The engine assumes the uninsured cost is debt-funded and that no waiver, cure right or equity injection is available [8].
VERDICT: PASS-TIGHT (EBITDA/interest)
CHECK NEXT: how much of the remaining headroom a larger loss, a lower margin or a slower insurance payment would use; also the business-interruption cover and its waiting period.
NOT IN THE SOURCES: the insurer's payment timing, any covenant waiver, and the company's actual response.

What is the delta-change method?

Delta change takes today's observed or modelled hazard and adjusts it by the change the climate models project, for example multiplying a flood depth by a factor derived from the rain increase. It is simple, transparent and keeps the local detail of the present-day data. Its weakness is that it assumes the pattern of weather stays the same: it cannot represent changes in storm tracks, timing or the shape of events, so it is best for screening, not final design.

What is the difference between a limit and a sublimit?

A limit caps what the policy pays for a loss; a sublimit caps one cause or coverage inside it, for example flood within a property policy. Limits truncate the top of the loss distribution, which lowers extreme-year losses and tail value at risk without touching small losses. A sublimit does the same for one peril only. When an insurer runs a model the limit and sublimit must be applied after the damage is converted to money and before losses are added across perils and sites.

How can heat affect industrial assets?

High air and water temperatures reduce the efficiency of power plants and cooling systems, raise electricity demand, limit safe working hours and can derate equipment such as transformers. Extended heat waves combine with drought to reduce cooling-water availability. The combined measure of temperature and humidity, such as wet-bulb temperature, matters for human limits, whereas dry-bulb temperature matters more for equipment. Impacts are site-specific and depend on design margins.

Which time horizon should I use for a loan or an asset?

Match the horizon to the life of the exposure. A five-year loan has little climate-driven change in hazard, so today's climate with a margin for model error is often enough. A 25-year plant or a 30-year mortgage justifies mid-century scenarios, and long-lived infrastructure should look beyond 2050. Use more than one pathway for the later horizons, because the differences between pathways grow with time.

What is the difference between ground-up loss and insured loss?

Ground-up loss is the full physical damage valued in money, before any policy terms. Insured loss is what remains after deductibles, limits and sublimits have been applied. The gap between them is the policyholder's retained loss. Comparing the two shows how much of the damage the terms push back onto the owner, which is useful both for insurers pricing the terms and for owners deciding whether to retain more risk or invest in protection.

What is a linked stress test and why not run each risk on its own?

A linked stress test follows one event through every consequence in time order and adds the costs together. A storm cuts the grid, a supplier is hit, a rush shipment goes by air, and the air shipment triggers a border tariff. Run separately, the freight premium looks like the price of avoiding a late-delivery penalty. Run together, the same decision also triggers the tariff, and the net can reverse. The engine runs each piece on its own as well, so a user can use only the part they need.

What is the difference between a limit and a sublimit?

A limit caps what the policy pays for a loss; a sublimit caps one cause or coverage inside it, for example flood within a property policy. Limits truncate the top of the loss distribution, which lowers extreme-year losses and tail value at risk without touching small losses. A sublimit does the same for one peril only. When an insurer runs a model the limit and sublimit must be applied after the damage is converted to money and before losses are added across perils and sites.

Only partly. Against Canadian fire records on unseen years the index separated large-fire days from other days of the season better than chance, but no better than the day's maximum temperature alone, and its probabilities add little over the calendar. What does demand surge mean?

Demand surge is the temporary rise in repair and rebuilding costs after a large catastrophe, caused by shortages of labour and materials. It makes the actual insured loss higher than the physical damage would suggest at normal prices. It matters most for very large regional events. A screening tool that values damage at normal prices will tend to understate the largest losses, so the 1-in-100 and 1-in-250 figures should be read as lower bounds on that point.
